definition: A flood with a 1-in-100 chance of happening in any given year. Climate Ready Boston found today's 1% flood would become a 10% chance by mid-century.
A three-digit number, now also an app and website, for non-emergency city services and information in the US and Canada.
The US three-digit number for mental health crisis calls, texts and chats, live since July 2022.
A crossing device with a locator tone, vibrating button, tactile arrow and spoken or audible walk cue for blind and low-vision pedestrians.
The concentration of a contaminant, such as lead, that triggers required steps by a water utility. Under the US LCRI it drops from 15 to 10 parts per billion for lead.
Signal operation where detectors decide whether a phase is served and how long it lasts.
A system that continually retunes splits, cycle lengths and offsets from live detector data instead of fixed plans.
Meters that report electricity use back to the utility automatically. Eversource told the Boston City Council it is installing them along with a distribution management system.
The hat-wearing walking-man pedestrian signal from East Germany, kept after reunification and now a Berlin symbol.
A sealed tank where bacteria break down sewage sludge without oxygen. Deer Island has 12 egg-shaped ones.

aka: automatic number identification / automatic location identification
definition: The caller's number and the address or location looked up for a legacy 911 call.
A channel that carries water by gravity from a distant source to a city. Most of Rome's ran underground or at ground level, not on arches.
An early electric light that makes a bright, harsh glow from a spark jumping between two carbon rods.
A controller that calculates local sunrise and sunset each day and switches lights accordingly.
Solar panels on a home or business that reduce the demand the grid sees rather than appearing as a power plant.
A pump that raises water pressure so water can reach upper floors or higher ground.
The body created by Massachusetts law in 1977, separate from the City of Boston, that runs Boston's local water, sewer and storm drain pipes and sets its own rates.
The unique number of a fire alarm box, which identifies its location to the alarm office.
Technical rules for how buildings must be built safely, covering structure, fire, plumbing, electrical and energy.
A system that shows the allowed speed inside the train cab instead of only on trackside lights.
A multi-year plan for building or repairing long-lived assets like schools, roads and pipes, usually paid for with borrowed money.
A building where many telecom networks place equipment and connect to each other. Boston's internet exchange runs at One Summer Street, a datacenter run by Markley Group.
A plant that generates electricity for many customers over a network of wires, instead of each building making its own.
An official document confirming that a finished building meets the codes and may be used.
A pit beneath or beside a building where human waste collected until someone emptied it.
A long-lasting disinfectant made by combining chlorine and ammonia that keeps water safe as it travels through the pipes.
Changes to infrastructure and planning that reduce harm from climate impacts like flooding and heat.
Boston's climate study, released in December 2016, that set out sea level rise and flood risk projections for the city.
A measure in kelvins of how warm (low K, yellow) or cool (high K, blue-white) a white light looks. The AMA recommended 3000K or lower for streets in 2016.
A single pipe network that carries both household sewage and street stormwater.
The release of untreated sewage and stormwater through a relief outfall when rain overloads a combined sewer.
In New York, one of 20 districts where only three authorized private carters may collect business trash, plus five citywide carters for large containers.
The bottom layer of a modern US landfill cell: a plastic geomembrane laid over two feet of compacted clay.
Requiring trash to go into sealed bins instead of bags on the sidewalk, largely to cut off food for rats.
Items that do not belong in a recycling bin, or recyclables too dirty to sell. China's National Sword set a 0.5% limit on it for scrap imports.
The small, ruggedized computer in a roadside cabinet that decides which movements get green and for how long.
The metal box at the corner of an intersection that holds the controller, detector cards, power and safety equipment.
Adjusting water chemistry, such as pH and alkalinity, so the water dissolves less lead and copper from old pipes.
Slow deformation of a material under constant load. Creep in epoxy adhesive let the Big Dig ceiling anchors pull out in 2006.
A site a utility restores ahead of ordinary customers after an outage. Eversource lists hospitals, police and fire stations, and water and sewage plants.
The time a signal takes to go through its complete sequence of phases once.
A voter-approved temporary tax increase that covers the loan payments on a specific capital project.
The Massachusetts nonprofit notification center that has utilities mark buried lines before anyone digs; notice is required 72 business hours ahead.
A detailed digital model of a city or system used to simulate and plan changes, such as Virtual Singapore.
Electricity that flows in one direction. Early systems like Pearl Street used low-voltage DC.
A street address plus details such as floor or apartment that responders can actually go to.
A medium-voltage line that carries power from a substation through a neighborhood.
The can on a pole, box on a pad or unit in a vault that lowers voltage to what buildings use.
A system that makes steam at central plants and pipes it under the streets to heat many buildings.
The government's power to take private property for public use, with payment to the owner.
A self-supporting government account, common for water and sewer, where user fees pay the system's costs instead of the property tax.
The IP network that carries NG911 traffic to call centers.
Vicinity Energy's name for steam made with electricity instead of by burning fuel.
A law that makes companies selling packaged products pay for collecting and recycling the packaging, usually through a producer responsibility organization.
Official permission for a utility to skip filtering its water because its protected source stays consistently clean.
A network of street boxes wired to a central office; pulling a box sends its number so the office knows where the alarm came from. Boston opened the first municipal system in 1852.
The US nationwide broadband network for public safety, run by AT&T on 700 MHz Band 14 under a 25-year contract.
An asphalt road surface laid on a base of angular crushed rock over the native soil.
A fused switch on a pole that disconnects a faulted transformer so one failure does not take down the whole line.
A valve that steps gas pressure down and opens or closes to hold the pressure downstream steady, often guided by a sensing line.
A worker in Tudor England who emptied privies and cesspits, allowed to work only between 9 pm and 5 am.
Pipes, tanks and tunnels that collect and store stormwater and sewage, as opposed to plant- and soil-based approaches.
Plant or soil systems and permeable surfaces, such as rain gardens and green roofs, that manage stormwater where it falls.
A string of signals timed so a vehicle at the planned speed meets green after green.
The Massachusetts program, created by a 2014 law, that lets gas utilities recover the cost of replacing leak-prone pipe.
A shared file format agencies use to publish routes, stops and schedules so any app can read them. It began with Portland's TriMet and Google in 2005.
A companion live feed that shares delays, vehicle positions and service alerts.
A discharge lamp with an orange-pink light that became the preferred street lamp in the late 20th century.
A layer of ice that forms between pavement and base in freezing weather; when it thaws it leaves a void under the road.
A public body created by law to run a system like transit, water or an airport, with its own board and budget, outside direct city control.
A coil of wire laid in sealed saw cuts in the pavement that detects a vehicle through the change in its inductance.
A large sewer that collects the flow of many smaller sewers before it reaches a river and carries it somewhere else.
Our term for the way city systems rely on each other, so that a failure in one, such as power, can spread to others, such as water pumps, signals and trains.
A shared switch where networks swap traffic directly; Boston's runs at One Summer Street.
The difference between what is needed to bring infrastructure to a good state of repair and what is actually being spent. ASCE put the US gap at $3.7 trillion over 10 years in 2025.

aka: Integrated Public Alert and Warning System
definition: FEMA's hub that relays authorized alerts to wireless carriers for broadcast to phones.

aka: independent system operator; regional transmission organization
definition: An organization that runs a region's high-voltage grid and wholesale electricity market, separate from the utilities that own local wires.
An upper floor that overhangs the floor below. London banned them after the 1666 fire.
Ground created by filling marshes or tidal flats with earth and gravel, as in Boston's Back Bay.
The liquid that seeps down through buried garbage; landfills collect and remove it from on top of the liner.
A 2024 US EPA rule requiring most water systems to replace lead service lines within 10 years, with replacement complete by December 31, 2037.
A 3-7 second walk signal shown before parallel traffic gets its green.
Old cast-iron or unprotected steel gas pipe that is prone to cracking and leaking. Massachusetts had 4,049 miles left in 2025.
Under Proposition 2½, an absolute cap on the property tax levy of 2.5% of the total assessed value of property in a town.
Under Proposition 2½, the most property tax a Massachusetts city may raise in a year. It grows 2.5% a year plus new growth from construction.
A device in a signal cabinet that turns the controller's 12-volt DC logic into the 120-volt AC power that lights the lamps.
An independent safety device that watches the signal outputs and forces the intersection into flash if it sees conflicting greens or bad voltages.
A fire, smoke or explosion in an underground electrical structure, most often caused by failing cable insulation.
A state authority created in 1985 that supplies wholesale water and sewage treatment to 61 municipalities in the Boston area.
A fire alarm box connected to a building such as a school, hospital or library that reports straight to the fire department.
A plant that sorts mixed recyclables into bales of paper, metal and plastic for sale.
A sulfur compound added to odorless natural gas so leaks smell like rotten eggs.
The old belief that diseases like cholera spread through foul-smelling air rather than through contaminated water.
Frank Sprague's invention that lets one operator control the motors in every car of a train at once.
A loan investors make to a state, city or public authority, repaid with interest over a set period, often to pay for capital projects.
Everyday trash from homes, schools, offices and shops, as distinct from industrial or hazardous waste.

aka: Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices
definition: The US federal rulebook for traffic signals, signs and markings; the 11th edition took effect in 2024.
US federal rules that set how often and how public bridges must be inspected, first published in 1971.
A Chinese policy launched in 2017 that in 2018 banned many scrap imports, including plastics, and set a 0.5% contamination limit.
A switch in an underground vault that opens when power would flow backward from the network into a dead primary feeder.
A US consensus standard for career fire departments setting turnout and travel time targets, such as 80 seconds turnout and 240 seconds travel for the first engine.
An internet-protocol 911 system that can carry voice, text, images and location embedded in the call.
Human waste collected from cesspits and privies, usually at night, and carted away, often to fertilize farmland.

aka: National Transportation Communications for ITS Protocol
definition: A family of US standards that lets central computers communicate with signal controllers and other roadside devices from different makers.
Federal money legally committed to a specific project, even if it has not yet been paid out.
The time relationship between a signal's cycle and a master clock, used to line up neighboring signals into a green wave.
A government website that publishes datasets for anyone to download and reuse, such as Analyze Boston.
Paying a fare by tapping your own bank card or phone instead of an agency-issued card.
An open standard API that lets apps submit and track service requests in city 311 systems.
The yearly spending plan for running services, such as salaries, fuel and supplies, paid mostly from taxes, fees and aid.
The pipe or tunnel end where treated wastewater, or a sewer overflow, is released into a body of water.
A wire strung above the track that a train touches with a pantograph or trolley pole to draw electricity. Boston's Green Line uses it.
A voter-approved permanent increase in a Massachusetts town's levy limit, passed by majority vote.
Disinfecting water with ozone gas, which kills microbes including tough parasites such as Cryptosporidium and Giardia.
A digital radio standard meant to let public safety radios from different makers work together.
Charging households by how much they throw away, for example through designated bags or bins that weigh food waste.
The highest amount of electricity used at one moment, which the grid must be built to meet. New England's record is 28,130 MW.
A setting that brings up the walk signal every cycle automatically, so the push button has no effect on timing.
A timed block of the signal cycle that serves one set of movements that can safely go together.
US stages for wireless 911 location: Phase I gives the cell tower, Phase II adds the caller's estimated coordinates.
A coating in a white LED that turns some of its blue light into yellow so the mix looks white. When it fails, the light can look purple.
A small light sensor that switches a streetlight on at dusk and off at dawn.
Underground tubes that use air to move trash from buildings to a central collection point, as on New York's Roosevelt Island since 1974.
A single identifiable source of pollution, such as a pipe, which the US Clean Water Act requires to have a permit.
A US bridge whose lowest-rated deck, superstructure, substructure or culvert scores 4 or less on a 0-9 scale.
Interrupting a signal's normal operation to give an immediate green to an emergency vehicle or clear a railroad crossing.
The white paint or stakes an excavator puts down to show where digging will happen, before notifying Dig Safe so utilities can mark their lines.
A section of a water system or tall building kept within a set pressure range by elevation, pumps or valves. In high-rises a zone typically spans 9 to 10 floors.
A valve that lowers water pressure to a safe level for the pipes and fixtures downstream.
Signal operation where every phase gets a set amount of time every cycle regardless of traffic.
The first stage of sewage treatment, where solids settle out of wastewater.
A nonprofit that collects fees from producers under an EPR law and runs or funds the recycling system. Circular Action Alliance is one in the US.
A 1980 Massachusetts law that caps how much property tax a city or town can raise, effective FY1982.
The call center that answers 911 calls.
A unit of water pressure. Each foot of water height adds about 0.433 psi.
A US rule allowing drivers to turn right after stopping at a red light unless a sign prohibits it.
The US way of diagramming phases: two rings of conflicting movements run side by side, and barriers keep conflicting movements in different rings from ever being timed together.
The amount of water a supply can reliably deliver every day, even through a long drought.
An engineered disposal site where waste is compacted and covered with soil, rather than left exposed as in an open dump.
A downtown underground grid in which many transformers feed one shared low-voltage mesh, so one failure does not cause an outage.
A second stage of sewage treatment, where bacteria break down dissolved organic pollution.
The phone-network switch in legacy 911 that sends each call to the correct PSAP.
A small pipe that tells a gas regulator the downstream pressure, so it knows whether to open or close.
The pipe that connects a building to the water main under the street.
A fitting with at least two inlets on a building's exterior where fire engines pump water into its standpipes or sprinklers.
The housing on a pole or mast arm that holds a signal's red, yellow and green lights.
A system where paper, cans, bottles and containers all go into one bin and are separated later at a sorting plant.
A stretch of track where trains must slow down because the track or its supports are in poor condition.
A low-power cell site, often on a streetlight or utility pole, that adds mobile capacity over a short range.
A city that uses sensors, data and software to manage services like traffic, energy and water.
An official city declaration that bans parking on main roads so plows can clear them; in Boston, cars left there are ticketed and towed.

An object such as a chair or cone placed in a shoveled parking spot to claim it. Boston tolerates them only during a declared snow emergency and for 48 hours after, and bans them in the South End and Bay Village.
A data message from a signal telling connected vehicles which light is showing and when it will change.
The share of the cycle given to one phase, usually including its yellow and all-red time.
Two or more transformers dedicated to a single large customer, for extra reliability.
A vertical pipe in a larger building that feeds hose valves firefighters connect to.
The orange-and-white tube placed over a manhole to vent steam above people and traffic.
A grid of metal columns and beams that carries a building's weight, so the outer walls no longer have to.
A movable gate across a river or estuary that closes to keep exceptionally high tides out of a city.
A rule barring utility digging in a recently rebuilt or resurfaced street, five years in Cambridge, Massachusetts, except in emergencies.
Scheduled mechanical cleaning of curbs, enforced with posted parking restrictions, tickets and tows.
A neighborhood built along streetcar lines, letting people live farther from work.
A city government in which an elected mayor runs the administration and proposes the budget, with the council acting mainly as a check.
The native soil a road is built on.
A low pit where water collects in a tunnel until pumps switch on at a set level. New York's subway has 300 pump rooms.
A 25 km storage tunnel under the Thames in London that intercepts 34 of the worst combined sewer overflows, opened in 2025.
A powered rail beside the running rails that a train touches with a sliding shoe to draw electricity. Boston's Red and Orange Lines use it.
A signal timing pattern switched by the clock, such as morning, off-peak, evening and overnight. Boston uses four default plans.
A facility that converts grid power into the direct current trains run on.
The control room where engineers watch cameras and adjust signal timing across a city.
A small timing adjustment, such as holding a green a few seconds longer, to help an approaching bus.
High-voltage lines that move power long distances from plants to substations. In New England this means 115 kV and above.
The body, created in 2000 under the Mayor of London, that runs London's Underground, buses, trams, main roads and congestion charge.
A trackside device that stops a train automatically if it runs a red signal.
The effect that makes cities hotter than surrounding countryside, because pavement and roofs absorb sun and there is less shade.
Mid-20th-century government programs that cleared neighborhoods labeled as blighted and redeveloped them, often displacing residents.
Passing water under ultraviolet light so microbes such as Cryptosporidium cannot reproduce.
Permission from a local board to build something that does not meet the zoning rules.
A road-safety policy that aims to eliminate all traffic deaths and serious injuries. Boston adopted it in 2015 with a 2030 target.
Burning trash in controlled plants to produce electricity and, in places like Copenhagen, heat for homes.
The land that drains rain and snowmelt into a particular river, lake or reservoir.
Government warnings broadcast from cell towers to phones in an area, with no app needed.
The vertical dimension of a caller's location, used to find the right floor in a tall building.
Local rules that set what kinds of buildings and uses are allowed on each piece of land, and how large they may be.
